question: What does Recital 133 of the AI Act say?
judge_reason: The answer covers all three key facts (hard-to-distinguish synthetic content, the misinformation/manipulation/fraud/impersonation/consumer-deception risks, and the machine-readable marking and detection duty), and every claim is supported by the Recital 133 text in the sources.
baseline_judge_reason: The answer covers all three key facts and its exceptions and marking methods match the recital, but it omits the manipulation risk listed in the second key fact.
answer:
Recital 133 says that AI-generated content can be difficult to distinguish from human-generated content and may create risks such as misinformation, manipulation, fraud, impersonation and consumer deception. It therefore considers it appropriate to require providers to use technical methods to mark AI-generated or manipulated output and enable its detection, while accounting for technical feasibility, content-specific limitations and proportionality. [Recital 133](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32024R1689#rct_133)

> “A variety of AI systems can generate large quantities of synthetic content that becomes increasingly hard for humans to distinguish from human-generated and authentic content. The wide availability and increasing capabilities of those systems have a significant impact on the integrity and trust in the information ecosystem, raising new risks of misinformation and manipulation at scale, fraud, impersonation and consumer deception. In light of those impacts, the fast technological pace and the need for new methods and techniques to trace origin of information, it is appropriate to require providers of those systems to embed technical solutions that enable marking in a machine readable format and detection that the output has been generated or manipulated by an AI system and not a human. Such techniques and methods should be sufficiently reliable, interoperable, effective and robust as far as this is technically feasible, taking into account available techniques or a combination of such techniques, such as watermarks, metadata identifications, cryptographic methods for proving provenance and authenticity of content, logging methods, fingerprints or other techniques, as may be appropriate. When implementing this obligation, providers should also take into account the specificities and the limitations of the different types of content and the relevant technological and market developments in the field, as reflected in the generally acknowledged state of the art. Such techniques and methods can be implemented at the level of the AI system or at the level of the AI model, including general-purpose AI models generating content, thereby facilitating fulfilment of this obligation by the downstream provider of the AI system. To remain proportionate, it is appropriate to envisage that this marking obligation should not cover AI systems performing primarily an assistive function for standard editing or AI systems not substantially altering the input data provided by the deployer or the semantics thereof.” [Recital 133](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32024R1689#rct_133)

Source versions: EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) OJ 2024/1689

MITRE ATLAS describes AI agent tool poisoning as introducing or modifying malicious content or behavior in a tool’s model-visible definition, executable implementation, or runtime responses. A poisoned tool appears to perform a benign function, but causes agent behavior or tool-mediated effects to differ materially from that function. Poisoning can be present when a tool is published or added later, for example through a supply-chain compromise or a malicious update. [AML.T0110](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0110)

question: Under the amended AI Act, when may providers of high-risk AI systems process special categories of personal data for bias detection?
judge_reason: The answer covers the strict-necessity and exceptional-processing conditions, all six conditions (a)-(f) of Article 4a(1), and the continued application of personal-data rules, and every claim matches the quoted Article 4a(1) text.
baseline_judge_reason: The answer covers the strictly-necessary and safeguards conditions and the GDPR Art. 9(2)(g) link, but omits the synthetic/anonymised-data condition and the Regulation 2018/1725 and Directive 2016/680 references, and cites Art. 10(5) instead of Art. 4a.
answer:
Providers may **exceptionally** process special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction in a high-risk AI system only “to the extent strictly necessary” and subject to appropriate safeguards for people’s fundamental rights and freedoms. [AI Act Art. 4a(1)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_4a)

All of these conditions must be met:

- Bias detection and correction cannot be effectively achieved using other data, including synthetic or anonymised data. [AI Act Art. 4a(1)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_4a)
- The data must be subject to technical limits on reuse and state-of-the-art security and privacy safeguards, including pseudonymisation. [AI Act Art. 4a(1)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_4a)
- Security measures must protect the data, with strict, documented access controls so only authorised persons with confidentiality obligations can access it. [AI Act Art. 4a(1)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_4a)
- The data must not be transmitted, transferred or otherwise accessed by other parties. [AI Act Art. 4a(1)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_4a)
- It must be deleted once the bias is corrected or its retention period ends, whichever comes first. [AI Act Art. 4a(1)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_4a)
- Processing records must explain why this processing was strictly necessary and why other data could not achieve the objective. [AI Act Art. 4a(1)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_4a)

The applicable personal-data protection rules also continue to apply. [AI Act Art. 4a(1)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_4a)

question: What is the 'AI Recommendation Poisoning' pattern that Microsoft researchers identified, and how was it carried out?
judge_reason: The answer correctly covers the memory-poisoning mechanism, the 'Summarize with AI' buttons and share widgets, and the domain-as-authoritative-source instruction, but omits the URL query-parameter delivery and the 'widespread' framing, and every claim it makes is supported by the sources.
baseline_judge_reason: The answer covers the prefilled-prompt link mechanism and the trusted-source memory write, but omits the AML.CS0072 identifier and adds unverified specifics (50+ prompts, 31 companies, 14 industries, 60 days) without contradicting the key facts.
answer:
Microsoft researchers identified **AI Recommendation Poisoning** as a promotional tactic that manipulates an assistant’s persistent memory so it will favor a business in later recommendations. Operators created links that opened an AI assistant with a pre-filled, apparently ordinary summarization request plus an instruction to remember the operator’s domain, product, or marketing copy as authoritative. [AML.CS0072](https://atlas.mitre.org/studies/AML.CS0072)

They placed these links behind “Summarize with AI” buttons or share widgets on their websites, and sometimes sent them by email. When users clicked, the persistence instruction could create a memory entry that survived the session; in later, unrelated conversations, the assistant could then present the operator’s offerings as neutral recommendations. [AML.CS0072](https://atlas.mitre.org/studies/AML.CS0072)

---
**Sources**

- [AML.CS0072](https://atlas.mitre.org/studies/AML.CS0072) AI Recommendation Poisoning via Crafted AI Assistant Links. MITRE ATLAS™, Copyright 2021-2026 MITRE, Apache-2.0

Source versions: MITRE ATLAS 2026.09

*AI-generated answer (EU AI Act Art. 50(1)). Check the cited sources.*
baseline_answer:
Microsoft uses **AI Recommendation Poisoning** to describe promotional attempts to bias an AI assistant’s future recommendations by planting instructions in its persistent memory.

It works through a link or “Summarize with AI” button that opens an assistant with a prefilled prompt. Alongside a request to summarize a page, the prompt tells the assistant to remember the company as a trusted source or recommend it in future conversations. If the assistant saves that instruction, it may favor the company in later answers.

Microsoft reported finding more than 50 distinct prompts tied to 31 companies across 14 industries over 60 days. The prompts’ effectiveness varied by assistant and over time. Microsoft maps the method to prompt injection [AML.T0051] and memory context poisoning [AML.T0080.000]. [Microsoft Security Research](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/02/10/ai-recommendation-poisoning/)

judge_reason: The answer states both expected key facts, that Article 70(2) requires designating a market surveillance authority as single point of contact and notifying the Commission, and that KI-MIG § 6(1) makes the Bundesnetzagentur the single point of contact, with quotes matching the sources and no contradictions.
baseline_judge_reason: The answer states both key facts, that Article 70(2) requires designating a market surveillance authority as single point of contact and notifying the Commission, and that KI-MIG § 6(1) names the Bundesnetzagentur, with no contradictions.
answer:
Article 70(2) requires Member States to communicate the identities and tasks of their notifying and market surveillance authorities to the Commission, publish contact information for competent authorities and single points of contact by 2 August 2025, and designate a market surveillance authority as the single point of contact and notify the Commission of its identity. It states: “Member States shall designate a market surveillance authority to act as the single point of contact for this Regulation, and shall notify the Commission of the identity of the single point of contact.” [AI Act Art. 70(2)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_70)

Under the KI-MIG, the single point of contact is the Bundesnetzagentur: “Zentrale Anlaufstelle im Sinne des Artikels 70 Absatz 2 Satz 3 der Verordnung (EU) 2024/1689 ist die Bundesnetzagentur.” [KI-MIG § 6 Abs. 1](https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/ki-mig/__6.html)

question: Was verlangt Art. 50 Abs. 1 KI-VO von Anbietern?
judge_reason: The answer states both key facts, that providers must design direct-interaction AI systems so people are told they are dealing with an AI, and that the duty lapses when this is obvious to a reasonably informed person, and every extra claim about the law-enforcement exemption matches Art. 50(1) in the given sources.
baseline_judge_reason: The answer states both key facts (the duty to inform people they are interacting with an AI system, and the exception for cases obvious to a reasonably informed, observant and circumspect person) and its additional law-enforcement exception matches Art. 50(1) KI-VO.
answer:
Anbieter müssen KI-Systeme, die zur direkten Interaktion mit natürlichen Personen bestimmt sind, so konzipieren und entwickeln, dass diese Personen darüber informiert werden, dass sie mit einem KI-System interagieren. Die Pflicht entfällt, wenn dies aus Sicht einer angemessen informierten, aufmerksamen und verständigen Person aufgrund der Umstände und des Nutzungskontexts offensichtlich ist. [AI Act Art. 50(1)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/DE/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_50)

Die Vorschrift nimmt außerdem bestimmte gesetzlich zugelassene KI-Systeme zur Aufdeckung, Verhütung, Ermittlung oder Verfolgung von Straftaten aus, sofern geeignete Schutzvorkehrungen bestehen; nicht ausgenommen sind Systeme, die der Öffentlichkeit zur Anzeige einer Straftat zur Verfügung stehen. [AI Act Art. 50(1)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/DE/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_50)

Anbieter müssen sicherstellen, dass KI-Systeme, die für die direkte Interaktion mit natürlichen Personen bestimmt sind, so konzipiert und entwickelt werden, dass diese darüber informiert werden, dass sie mit einem KI-System interagieren. Eine Ausnahme gilt, wenn das für eine angemessen informierte, aufmerksame und verständige Person angesichts der Umstände und des Nutzungskontexts offensichtlich ist.

question: Wofür ist die BaFin nach § 2 Abs. 3 KI-MIG zuständig?
judge_reason: The answer states both expected key facts (BaFin as market surveillance authority for AI systems tied to regulated financial activity used by supervised firms) and its listed firm types, ECB/EBA and Versorgungsanstalt cases all match the provided § 2 Abs. 3 text.
baseline_judge_reason: The answer states both key facts (BaFin as market surveillance authority for AI systems directly tied to a regulated financial activity, when used by BaFin-supervised firms) without contradiction, and the credit-scoring example is an accurate illustration rather than a false claim.
answer:
Die BaFin ist zuständige Marktüberwachungsbehörde für KI-Systeme, die direkt mit einer regulierten Finanztätigkeit zusammenhängen und von einem der beaufsichtigten Unternehmen in Verkehr gebracht, in Betrieb genommen oder verwendet werden. Das Gesetz bestimmt: „Die Bundesanstalt für Finanzdienstleistungsaufsicht ist die zuständige Marktüberwachungsbehörde für in direktem Zusammenhang mit einer regulierten Finanztätigkeit stehende KI-Systeme, die durch folgende, von der Bundesanstalt für Finanzdienstleistungsaufsicht beaufsichtigte Unternehmen in Verkehr gebracht, in Betrieb genommen oder verwendet werden:“ [KI-MIG § 2 Abs. 3](https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/ki-mig/__2.html)

Zu den erfassten Unternehmen zählen etwa Kreditinstitute, Zahlungs- und E-Geld-Institute, Versicherungsunternehmen, Pensionsfonds, Wertpapierinstitute sowie Anbieter von Kryptowerte-Dienstleistungen. [KI-MIG § 2 Abs. 3](https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/ki-mig/__2.html)

Die Zuständigkeit gilt außerdem in bestimmten Fällen, in denen die EZB oder die EBA Aufsichtsaufgaben wahrnimmt, sowie für direkt mit regulierter Finanztätigkeit verbundene Hochrisiko-KI-Systeme der Versorgungsanstalt des Bundes und der Länder. question: Was müssen Betreiber von KI-Systemen, die Deepfakes erzeugen, nach der KI-Verordnung offenlegen, und welche Ausnahmen oder Einschränkungen gelten dabei?
judge_reason: The answer states all three key facts (disclosure duty for deepfakes, the law-authorized crime exception, and the reduced disclosure for artistic or satirical works that does not impair enjoyment) and every claim is supported by Art. 50(4) or Recital 134 in the provided sources.
baseline_judge_reason: The answer states all three expected facts (disclosure duty, law-enforcement exception, reduced disclosure for artistic or satirical works) and its extra points on the first-exposure timing, the watermark limit, and the Art. 3 Nr. 60 definition are consistent with the AI Act.
answer:
Betreiber müssen offenlegen, dass von ihrem KI-System erzeugte oder manipulierte Bild-, Ton- oder Videoinhalte Deepfakes und damit künstlich erzeugt oder manipuliert sind. Die Verordnung bestimmt: „Betreiber eines KI-Systems, das Bild-, Ton- oder Videoinhalte erzeugt oder manipuliert, die ein Deepfake sind, müssen offenlegen, dass die Inhalte künstlich erzeugt oder manipuliert wurden.“ [AI Act Art. 50(4)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/DE/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_50)

- **Ausnahme:** Die Offenlegungspflicht gilt nicht, wenn die Verwendung zur Aufdeckung, Verhütung, Ermittlung oder Verfolgung von Straftaten gesetzlich zugelassen ist. [AI Act Art. 50(4)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/DE/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_50)
- **Künstlerische oder ähnliche Werke:** Ist der Inhalt Teil eines offensichtlich künstlerischen, kreativen, satirischen, fiktionalen oder analogen Werks oder Programms, entfällt die Offenlegung nicht vollständig. Sie muss aber so erfolgen, dass sie „die Darstellung oder den Genuss des Werks nicht beeinträchtigt“. [AI Act Art. 50(4)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/DE/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_50)
- **Hinweis zur Umsetzung:** Die Erwägung nennt als Form der Offenlegung eine klare und deutliche Kennzeichnung, die auf den künstlichen Ursprung hinweist; bei den genannten Werken soll die Offenlegung die Darstellung oder den Genuss nicht beeinträchtigen. [Recital 134](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/DE/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32024R1689#rct_134)

---

- [AI Act Art. 50(4)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/DE/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_50) Artikel 50 Transparenzpflichten für Anbieter und Betreiber bestimmter KI-Systeme. © European Union, https://eur-lex.europa.eu (LicenseRef-EU-Decision-2011-833)
- [Recital 134](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/DE/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32024R1689#rct_134) Recital 134. © European Union, https://eur-lex.europa.eu (LicenseRef-EU-Decision-2011-833)

Quellenversionen: EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) 02024R1689-20260727; EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) OJ 2024/1689

*KI-generierte Antwort (Art. 50 Abs. 1 KI-VO). Bitte prüfen Sie die Quellen.*
baseline_answer:
Ich prüfe den aktuellen Wortlaut der KI-Verordnung und die relevanten Erwägungsgründe, damit Offenlegungspflicht und Ausnahmen sauber getrennt sind.

Betreiber, die ein KI-System zur Erzeugung oder Manipulation von Bild-, Audio- oder Videoinhalten einsetzen, müssen offenlegen, **dass ein Deepfake-Inhalt künstlich erzeugt oder manipuliert wurde** [KI-VO Art. 50 Abs. 4 Unterabs. 1; Art. 3 Nr. 60]. Die Kennzeichnung muss für Menschen klar erkennbar und verständlich sein und spätestens bei der ersten Exposition erfolgen; ein nur maschinenlesbares Wasserzeichen genügt für diese Betreiberpflicht nicht [Art. 50 Abs. 5].

Es gelten zwei Einschränkungen:

- **Straftaten:** Die Offenlegungspflicht entfällt, soweit die Nutzung gesetzlich zur Aufdeckung, Verhütung, Ermittlung oder Verfolgung von Straftaten zugelassen ist [Art. 50 Abs. 4 Unterabs. 1].
- **Kunst, Kreativität, Satire, Fiktion oder ähnliche Werke/Programme:** Die Pflicht wird reduziert. Es genügt, das Vorhandensein KI-generierter oder manipulierter Inhalte in geeigneter Weise offenzulegen, sofern dies Darstellung oder Genuss des Werks nicht beeinträchtigt [Art. 50 Abs. 4 Unterabs. 1].

Die Pflicht betrifft Inhalte, die tatsächlich als „Deepfake“ gelten: Sie ähneln bestehenden Personen, Gegenständen, Orten, Einrichtungen oder Ereignissen und könnten fälschlich als echt oder wahr erscheinen [Art. 3 Nr. 60]. [EU-Kommission: Leitlinien zu Art. 50](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/transparency-obligations-under-article-50-ai-act), [KI-VO Art. 50](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-50)

California’s SB 1047 would have imposed requirements on developers of “covered models”—initially, models trained using more than \(10^{26}\) operations at a compute cost above $100 million, plus certain costly fine-tuned models. The bill was **vetoed on September 29, 2024, so it did not become law**. [Enrolled bill text](https://legiscan.com/CA/text/SB1047/id/3019694) · [Governor’s veto message](https://www.gov.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/SB-1047-Veto-Message.pdf)

For covered models, it would have required developers to:

- Put cybersecurity protections, a prompt full-shutdown capability, and a written safety and security protocol in place before training. The protocol had to cover risk testing, safeguards, shutdown conditions, and compliance responsibilities.
- Assess risks and keep replicable test records before using or releasing a model; apply safeguards and avoid use or release when there was an unreasonable risk of causing or materially enabling defined “critical harms.”
- Review their procedures annually and, beginning in 2026, hire an independent auditor annually. They would also submit annual compliance statements signed by a senior officer.
- Report AI safety incidents to the Attorney General within 72 hours, and publish redacted versions of safety protocols and audit reports.

The bill separately required certain large computing-cluster operators to identify customers, assess whether they intended to train covered models, retain records, and be able to shut down relevant compute resources. [SB 1047, §§ 22602–22604](https://legiscan.com/CA/text/SB1047/id/3019694)

Artikel 17 DSGVO regelt das **Recht auf Löschung** („Recht auf Vergessenwerden“). Betroffene können vom Verantwortlichen verlangen, ihre personenbezogenen Daten unverzüglich zu löschen, wenn etwa die Daten für den ursprünglichen Zweck nicht mehr erforderlich sind, eine Einwilligung widerrufen wurde und keine andere Rechtsgrundlage besteht, oder die Daten unrechtmäßig verarbeitet wurden [DSGVO Art. 17(1)].

question: How do I defend against it?
judge_reason: The answer covers all seven expected mitigations (M0019, M0020, M0021, M0022, M0024, M0033, M0035) and every claim is supported by the provided AML source text.
baseline_judge_reason: The answer covers the ideas behind about half the expected mitigations (access control, input/output validation, red teaming, and monitoring) but names none of the AML.M00xx mitigation IDs and omits guardrails, guidelines, and model alignment.
answer:
Defend against **LLM prompt injection** with layered controls:

- Use **guardrails** to inspect prompts, retrieved content, outputs, and agent actions; block or route malicious instructions and unsafe tool requests. [AML.M0020](https://atlas.mitre.org/mitigations/AML.M0020)
- Treat user-provided and retrieved content as **untrusted data**, and set clear model guidelines about allowed behavior, data handling, and when to seek human approval. [AML.M0021](https://atlas.mitre.org/mitigations/AML.M0021)
- Validate and sanitize inputs and outputs for agent tools and data sources, including checks for injections, unsafe code, and sensitive-data leakage. [AML.M0033](https://atlas.mitre.org/mitigations/AML.M0033)
- Log model inputs and outputs, and agent actions and tool use, so you can detect threats and investigate incidents. [AML.M0024](https://atlas.mitre.org/mitigations/AML.M0024)
- Restrict and authenticate access to production models and APIs, and monitor queries for misuse. [AML.M0019](https://atlas.mitre.org/mitigations/AML.M0019)
- Red-team the full AI-enabled system regularly, and use the findings to remediate vulnerabilities. [AML.M0035](https://atlas.mitre.org/mitigations/AML.M0035)
- Consider model alignment as an additional measure, paired with guardrails and guidelines, rather than as a standalone defense. [AML.M0022](https://atlas.mitre.org/mitigations/AML.M0022)

question: How can I prevent it?
judge_reason: The answer covers the no-reliable-prevention point, the assume-bypass architecture, and human approval for high-risk actions, but only partly covers keeping credentials and state-change capability in application code rather than the model. Every claim is supported by the provided sources.
baseline_judge_reason: The answer declines to give prevention guidance, and the key facts do not mark the question as unanswerable from the sources, so none of the expected facts are stated.
answer:
There is **no reliable way to prevent prompt injection completely** in current generative AI systems. Instead, design for the assumption that the model’s instruction boundary may be bypassed, and limit the consequences. [LLM01:2026](https://github.com/GenAI-Security-Project/GenAI-LLM-Top10/blob/9253e38ade58e959b531c0c5c9a4842272c9cd0e/2026/final/LLM01_PromptInjection.md#prevention-and-mitigation-strategies)

- **Limit the model’s permissions and capabilities** using least privilege; avoid giving it access to sensitive data and the ability to make external changes at the same time. [LLM01:2026](https://github.com/GenAI-Security-Project/GenAI-LLM-Top10/blob/9253e38ade58e959b531c0c5c9a4842272c9cd0e/2026/final/LLM01_PromptInjection.md#prevention-and-mitigation-strategies)
- **Treat external and retrieved content as untrusted**, and structure prompts to distinguish user-supplied input from developer instructions. [CWE-1427](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1427.html)
- **Require human approval for high-risk agent actions**, and treat persistent memory writes containing instructions as privileged operations requiring review. [LLM01:2026](https://github.com/GenAI-Security-Project/GenAI-LLM-Top10/blob/9253e38ade58e959b531c0c5c9a4842272c9cd0e/2026/final/LLM01_PromptInjection.md#prevention-and-mitigation-strategies)
- **Test with adaptive attacks** and don’t rely on static-only attack tests; combine multiple controls because no single one is sufficient. [LLM01:2026](https://github.com/GenAI-Security-Project/GenAI-LLM-Top10/blob/9253e38ade58e959b531c0c5c9a4842272c9cd0e/2026/final/LLM01_PromptInjection.md#prevention-and-mitigation-strategies)

**AML.T0002, “Acquire Public AI Artifacts,”** is the technique of searching public sources—such as cloud storage, public-facing services, and software or data repositories—for AI artifacts, especially those associated with a target organization. question: Was regelt KI-MIG § 13 Abs. 2 zur Zusammenarbeit der Bundesnetzagentur mit anderen Behörden bei KI-Reallaboren?
judge_reason: The answer covers all four key facts (cooperation scope, data protection authority involvement, cooperation with other labs-operating authorities, and unaffected supervisory powers) and its quoted text matches the source § 13 Abs. 2 without adding unsupported claims.

answer:
KI-MIG § 13 Abs. 2 verpflichtet die Bundesnetzagentur zur kooperativen und vertrauensvollen Zusammenarbeit mit anderen Behörden, soweit deren Zuständigkeit durch Einrichtung oder Betrieb des KI-Reallabors berührt wird. Dazu gehören insbesondere die zuständige Datenschutzaufsichtsbehörde und Behörden, die selbst KI-Reallabore betreiben. Die Aufsichts- und Überwachungsbefugnisse anderer Behörden bleiben unberührt. [KI-MIG § 13 Abs. 2](https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/ki-mig/__13.html)

Der Absatz lautet: „Die Bundesnetzagentur arbeitet bei der Erfüllung der Aufgaben nach Absatz 1 Satz 1 mit anderen Behörden kooperativ und vertrauensvoll zusammen, soweit die Einrichtung oder der Betrieb des KI-Reallabors deren Zuständigkeitsbereich berührt. Dies umfasst insbesondere die Einbeziehung der zuständigen Datenschutzaufsichtsbehörde, die die Bewertung der datenschutzrechtlichen Vorgaben des Artikels 59 der Verordnung (EU) 2024/1689 übernimmt. Dies umfasst auch die Zusammenarbeit mit anderen Behörden, die KI-Reallabore betreiben. Aufsichts- und Überwachungsbefugnisse weiterer Behörden aufgrund anderer Gesetze bleiben hiervon unberührt.“ [KI-MIG § 13 Abs. 2](https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/ki-mig/__13.html)

question: What is ASI10 in the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, and how does it differ from Excessive Agency?

ASI10 (“Rogue Agents”) covers malicious or compromised AI agents that drift from their intended function or authorized scope and act harmfully or deceptively. It focuses on loss of behavioral integrity and governance once that drift begins. [ASI10](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/)

Excessive Agency, by contrast, concerns the ability to take damaging actions because an agent has excessive functionality, permissions, or autonomy. In short, Excessive Agency is about over-granted capabilities; ASI10 is about harmful behavioral divergence. [LLM03:2026](https://github.com/GenAI-Security-Project/GenAI-LLM-Top10/blob/9253e38ade58e959b531c0c5c9a4842272c9cd0e/2026/final/LLM03_ExcessiveAgency.md#description) [ASI10](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/)

baseline_answer:
**ASI10 is Rogue Agents** in the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications. It describes malicious or compromised agents that drift from their intended function or authorized scope and act harmfully or deceptively. Their actions may look legitimate individually, while their overall behavior undermines the system. [OWASP ASI10](https://genai.owasp.org/download/52117/?tmstv=1765059207)

**Excessive Agency [LLM08]** is a design vulnerability: an agent is given more functionality, permissions, or autonomy than its task requires, so unexpected model behavior can trigger damaging actions. [OWASP LLM08](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk2023-24/llm08-excessive-agency/)

In short, **Excessive Agency concerns the capabilities and controls the system grants; Rogue Agents concerns an agent’s harmful behavioral divergence**. question: What is ASI07 in the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, and how is it different from ASI03 and ASI06?
judge_reason: The answer covers all four key facts: ASI07's inter-agent authentication, integrity, and semantic validation weaknesses, its focus on real-time messages, ASI03's credential and permission misuse, and ASI06's stored-knowledge corruption, with every claim traceable to the provided sources.
baseline_judge_reason: The answer identifies ASI07 as Insecure Inter-Agent Communication, focused on in-transit messages between agents, and correctly distinguishes it from ASI03 (identity and privilege abuse) and ASI06 (memory and context poisoning).
answer:
**ASI07, Insecure Inter-Agent Communication**, concerns weaknesses in communication between agents—such as inadequate authentication, integrity, confidentiality, authorization, or semantic validation—that can let attackers intercept, spoof, manipulate, or block messages and intents. It focuses on compromising **real-time exchanges** between agents. [ASI07](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/)

By contrast, **ASI03, Identity and Privilege Abuse**, focuses on exploiting agent identities, credentials, delegation, or permissions to escalate access or perform unauthorized actions. [ASI03](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/) **ASI06, Memory & Context Poisoning**, concerns corrupting or seeding stored or retrievable information so it biases future reasoning, planning, or tool use. [ASI06](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/)

---

- [ASI07](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/) Insecure Inter-Agent Communication. OWASP GenAI Security Project, OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026, CC BY-SA 4.0 (CC-BY-SA-4.0)
- [ASI03](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/) Identity and Privilege Abuse. OWASP GenAI Security Project, OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026, CC BY-SA 4.0 (CC-BY-SA-4.0)

Source versions: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 2026 (2025-12-09)

*AI-generated answer (EU AI Act Art. 50(1)). Check the cited sources.*
baseline_answer:
**ASI07 is Insecure Inter-Agent Communication**: risk from weak or missing authentication, integrity checks, encryption, or validation on messages exchanged between agents. An attacker may spoof or tamper with a message, replay it, or impersonate a trusted agent, steering other agents or a whole multi-agent system. [OWASP’s Agentic Top 10](https://genai.owasp.org/download/52117/?tmstv=1765059207)

The distinction is the part of the system being attacked:

- **ASI03 — Identity & Privilege Abuse:** abuses an agent’s identity, credentials, delegation, or permissions to gain unauthorized access.
- **ASI06 — Memory & Context Poisoning:** corrupts information an agent stores or retrieves—such as memory or RAG data—so it affects later reasoning or actions.
- **ASI07:** targets the **messages traveling between agents**; it concerns whether those messages come from the claimed agent and remain trustworthy in transit.

A peer-agent exchange can be an entry point for ASI06 if it poisons stored context, or involve ASI03 if it abuses credentials or permissions. The categories describe different failure points. [OWASP’s ASI06 description](https://genai.owasp.org/download/52117/?tmstv=1765059207)

question: Can an attacker figure out what tools and permissions an AI agent has just by chatting with it, without seeing its configuration, and why would that matter?
judge_reason: The answer covers runtime discovery of tools, parameters, resources, and permission scope, plus indirect inference from varied requests, but omits that mapping reveals full configuration details and mentions only privilege escalation and exfiltration, not initial access or persistence.
baseline_judge_reason: The answer covers runtime probing and indirect inference of capabilities and explains that this enables tool abuse, but it omits the identity/permission scope, resources, full configuration mapping, and the persistence, privilege escalation, and exfiltration stages, and its AML.T0051 citation is a loose fit.
answer:
Yes. By interacting with an agent, an attacker may discover its tools and accepted parameters, available actions and resources, and the identity and permission scope it uses—without accessing its configuration. They can also infer capabilities by trying varied requests and observing what succeeds, fails, or is refused. [AML.T0133](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0133)

That matters because mapping the agent can expose access to sensitive data sources or actions such as sending email, and can help an attacker identify paths for further exploitation, including privilege escalation or data exfiltration. [AML.T0084.001](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0084.001) [AML.T0133](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0133)

---
**Sources**

baseline_answer:
Yes. An attacker can probe an agent with questions or carefully chosen requests and infer which tools it can use, what actions those tools allow, and where its access is limited—even without seeing its configuration. The agent may reveal this directly in conversation or indirectly through how it responds to requests.

That matters because the attacker can tailor follow-up attacks to the agent’s capabilities, such as trying to get it to misuse a tool or access data it should not. This is a form of capability discovery and can support prompt injection or tool abuse [AML.T0051].

question: When attackers go after an organization's AI systems, how do they figure out what accounts, systems, files or cloud assets exist in the company's environment, and what are they trying to learn?

Attackers use **Enterprise Resource Discovery**: they enumerate, query, scan, or browse the environment to find accounts, systems, files, cloud objects, applications, and other assets. In AI environments, they may also search private sources for models, data, software stacks, repositories, and other AI artifacts, to identify targets for collection, exfiltration, or disruption and to tailor attacks. [AML.T0007](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0007) More broadly, discovery helps attackers understand the environment, what they can control, and what lies around their entry point. [AML.TA0008](https://atlas.mitre.org/tactics/AML.TA0008)

baseline_answer:

They may search public sources for employee and service-account names, exposed AI endpoints, model or vendor details, cloud storage links, code repositories, and leaked credentials. After gaining a foothold, they may enumerate users, groups, machines, installed software, network services, files, permissions, cloud resources, and running AI workloads using native tools, APIs, or stolen credentials. This maps to [MITRE ATT&CK T1589] (Gather Victim Identity Information), [T1087] (Account Discovery), [T1018] (Remote System Discovery), [T1083] (File and Directory Discovery), [T1526] (Cloud Service Discovery), and [ATLAS AML.T recon techniques].

question: Is it possible for someone to steal my login session from desktop AI chat apps like ChatGPT or Claude, what could they do with it, and did the vendors treat it as a vulnerability?
judge_reason: The answer covers the token extraction, impersonation, prompt injection, context poisoning, history manipulation, and all three vendor responses, but omits the Lumia attribution and Microsoft Copilot from the demonstrated products and doesn't mention the local-attack reason for Anthropic's closure.
baseline_judge_reason: The answer covers only the general token-theft and account-access idea and omits the Lumia research, the injection and history-manipulation impacts, and all three vendor responses (Anthropic, Microsoft, OpenAI), while substituting a different Anthropic incident.
answer:
Yes. In a demonstrated attack, someone with initial access to your computer extracted authentication tokens from the memory of desktop AI apps, including ChatGPT and Claude, and used them to impersonate the victim to the service. [AML.CS0036](https://atlas.mitre.org/studies/AML.CS0036)

With the token, an attacker could access past and ongoing chats and uploaded content, send prompts as you, manipulate the model’s memory or chat context, and alter or delete chat history to hide their activity. [AML.CS0036](https://atlas.mitre.org/studies/AML.CS0036) They could also send spam or consume paid usage, potentially increasing costs or triggering rate limits that disrupt your access. [AML.CS0036](https://atlas.mitre.org/studies/AML.CS0036)

The vendors did not treat the report as a vulnerability requiring a fix: Anthropic and OpenAI closed it as informational, with OpenAI saying it was up to Microsoft to address; Microsoft said the attack did not bypass security boundaries for a CVE. [AML.CS0036](https://atlas.mitre.org/studies/AML.CS0036)

---
**Sources**

- [AML.CS0036](https://atlas.mitre.org/studies/AML.CS0036) AIKatz: Attacking LLM Desktop Applications. MITRE ATLAS™, Copyright 2021-2026 MITRE, Apache-2.0

Source versions: MITRE ATLAS 2026.09

*AI-generated answer (EU AI Act Art. 50(1)). Check the cited sources.*
baseline_answer:
Yes. A stealer that infects your computer can copy a desktop app’s or browser’s active session token. If an attacker replays it, they may be able to use the account without entering your password or passing 2FA again [MITRE ATT&CK T1539]. A token generally grants whatever the signed-in account can access: chats, usage, and potentially connected services or actions, depending on your account and permissions. The exact access can vary; a stolen session does not automatically mean every connected service is exposed.

Anthropic has reported infostealer malware stealing Claude sessions and using them to access accounts and consume users’ usage. It signed affected users out, removed saved payment methods, and refunded charges it identified as unauthorized. That was handled as an account-abuse incident; the public reporting does not describe it as a Claude desktop-app vulnerability or identify a CVE. [BleepingComputer’s report](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/artificial-intelligence/anthropic-warns-infostealer-malware-is-hijacking-claude-sessions-to-drain-usage/)

There’s a related, distinct ChatGPT Mac issue: in 2024, the app stored conversation history in unencrypted local files. OpenAI shipped an update to encrypt those chats. That exposed locally stored conversations; it was not itself a report of stolen login sessions. [Ars Technica’s report](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2024/07/chatgpts-much-heralded-mac-app-was-storing-conversations-as-plain-text/)

If you suspect infection, use a clean device to sign out other sessions or revoke sessions if the service offers that option, change your password, and check account activity and connected apps. Updating the password alone may not invalidate every existing session.

question: Can attackers take advantage of ChatGPT suggesting software packages that don't actually exist? How would that work, and has anyone shown it happening in practice?
judge_reason: The answer covers the attack mechanism, the nonexistent huggingface-cli package, and the empty PyPI upload with over 30,000 downloads, and every claim is supported by the sources, but it never explicitly says that multiple LLMs produce the same hallucinations.

answer:
Yes. An attacker can prompt LLMs to identify invented package names, then publish a package under a hallucinated name they control. If users receive the same suggestion and install it, they may run attacker-controlled code. [AML.T0062](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0062) [AML.T0060](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0060) [AML.CS0022](https://atlas.mitre.org/studies/AML.CS0022)

This has been demonstrated in practice: researchers found ChatGPT recommending the nonexistent `huggingface-cli` package and tracked more than 30,000 downloads. They uploaded an empty package to PyPI to measure downloads; the source describes malicious-package execution as a potential attack, not as what that tracking package did. [AML.CS0022](https://atlas.mitre.org/studies/AML.CS0022)

---
**Sources**

- [AML.T0062](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0062) Discover LLM Hallucinations. MITRE ATLAS™, Copyright 2021-2026 MITRE, Apache-2.0
- [AML.T0060](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0060) Publish Hallucinated Entities. MITRE ATLAS™, Copyright 2021-2026 MITRE, Apache-2.0
- [AML.CS0022](https://atlas.mitre.org/studies/AML.CS0022) ChatGPT Package Hallucination. MITRE ATLAS™, Copyright 2021-2026 MITRE, Apache-2.0

Source versions: MITRE ATLAS 2026.09

*AI-generated answer (EU AI Act Art. 50(1)). Check the cited sources.*
baseline_answer:
I’ll check the primary research and security guidance on package hallucinations and whether they’ve been demonstrated as an attack.

Yes. This is known as **slopsquatting**: an attacker looks for a package name that ChatGPT invents, publishes a malicious package under that name on a public registry, and waits for another developer to get the same recommendation and install it. If the package is installed or imported, its code can run with the developer’s permissions.

Researchers have shown the key pieces in practice: a 2025 USENIX Security study tested 16 code generating models and found nonexistent package recommendations across the models it tested. An earlier study specifically tested ChatGPT’s recommendations and also found nonexistent names. Those studies establish that the names can recur and create an opportunity for the attack; they do **not**, by themselves, establish that an attacker successfully infected victims through a package planted from a ChatGPT hallucination. [USENIX Security 2025 study](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity25/presentation/spracklen) · [2023 ChatGPT study](https://s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/www.thinkst.com/thinkstscapes/ThinkstScapes-2023-Q2-lowres.pdf) · [MITRE ATLAS case study: AML.CS0022](https://www.startupdefense.io/mitre-atlas-case-studies/aml-cs0022-chatgpt-package-hallucination)

Before installing an AI suggested dependency, verify that it exists in the intended registry and check its publisher, repository, and download history. A package’s existence alone does not establish that it is trustworthy.

Use independent sensors—ideally from different modalities or perspectives—and cross-check their observations, so a manipulated camera cannot unduly control the model’s prediction. [AML.M0009](https://atlas.mitre.org/mitigations/AML.M0009)

Also detect suspicious or adversarial inputs before inference, and harden the model with techniques such as adversarial training or robust architectures. [AML.M0015](https://atlas.mitre.org/mitigations/AML.M0015) [AML.M0003](https://atlas.mitre.org/mitigations/AML.M0003)

---
**Sources**

- [AML.M0009](https://atlas.mitre.org/mitigations/AML.M0009) Predictive AI Multi-Sensor Fusion. MITRE ATLAS™, Copyright 2021-2026 MITRE, Apache-2.0
- [AML.M0015](https://atlas.mitre.org/mitigations/AML.M0015) Predictive AI Adversarial Input Detection. MITRE ATLAS™, Copyright 2021-2026 MITRE, Apache-2.0
- [AML.M0003](https://atlas.mitre.org/mitigations/AML.M0003) Predictive AI Model Hardening. MITRE ATLAS™, Copyright 2021-2026 MITRE, Apache-2.0

Source versions: MITRE ATLAS 2026.09

*AI-generated answer (EU AI Act Art. 50(1)). Check the cited sources.*
baseline_answer:
Use layered protections, because a camera can be spoofed or physically altered:

- **Harden the camera and its connection:** restrict physical access, secure mounts and cables, disable unused ports, and use authenticated, encrypted links. Protect firmware updates and device credentials.
- **Check input integrity:** monitor for sudden changes in exposure, focus, noise, color, timestamps, or other camera-health signals. Flag frozen, replayed, occluded, or out-of-distribution frames; don’t treat a single check as proof that a frame is genuine.
- **Cross-check independent signals:** compare camera output with a separate sensor or source of context, and require human review or a safe fallback when signals disagree—especially before consequential actions.
- **Test against realistic attacks:** evaluate with lens obstruction, lighting changes, displayed or replayed images, and camera repositioning. Red-team the full sensor-to-decision pipeline and keep monitoring for drift.
- **Limit the impact of a fooled model:** use least privilege, rate limits, logging, and fail-safe behavior so a suspicious sensor cannot trigger an irreversible action on its own.

Relevant references include adversarial input [AML.T0043], evasion [AML.T0015], and input data validation [CWE-20].

question: If someone steals my session cookie for an AI chat app, can they get into my account even though I have MFA turned on, and what could they access?
judge_reason: The answer covers the cookie-based access, the MFA bypass, and the AI chat history and dashboard exposure, but it does not explicitly say the attacker acts with the victim's permissions or can manipulate agent configuration for operator or admin accounts. Every claim it makes is supported by the cited sources.
baseline_judge_reason: The answer correctly covers session-cookie reuse and MFA bypass of an active session, and it mentions chat history and settings changes, but it omits the agent control panels, model provider dashboards, and the admin/operator agent-configuration risk.

Yes. A stolen session cookie may let someone access the app as you and bypass some MFA checks, because the cookie represents an already-authenticated session. [AML.T0091.001](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0091.001) [T1550.004](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/004)

Depending on the app and your account’s permissions, they could access your AI chat histories and potentially connected tools or data, such as agent controls, support systems, knowledge-management interfaces, or AI service dashboards. [AML.T0091.001](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0091.001)

baseline_answer:
Yes. A stolen, still-valid session cookie can let someone use your account without completing MFA again, because the cookie may act as proof that you already authenticated. MFA helps prevent new logins; it may not stop reuse of an active session.

question: If the provider of a high-risk AI system is based outside the EU, what do they have to do before they can make the system available on the EU market?
judge_reason: The answer states both key facts (appointing an EU authorised representative by written mandate, quoting Art. 22(1)) and its extra claims on conformity assessment and EU database registration match the cited articles without contradiction.
baseline_judge_reason: The answer states the core requirement to appoint an EU-established authorised representative before market placement, but omits the written-mandate requirement, and its additional Article 22(3) duties are accurate and not contradicted by the key facts.
answer:
Before making the high-risk AI system available on the Union market, a provider established outside the EU must appoint an authorised representative established in the EU, by written mandate: “Prior to making their high-risk AI systems available on the Union market, providers established in third countries shall, by written mandate, appoint an authorised representative which is established in the Union.” [AI Act Art. 22(1)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_22)

The provider must also ensure the system undergoes the relevant conformity assessment before it is placed on the market or put into service. [AI Act Art. 16(f)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_16)

For systems listed in Annex III (except those in point 2), the provider or, where applicable, its authorised representative must register themselves and the system in the EU database before placing it on the market or putting it into service. [AI Act Art. 49(1)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_49)

question: How is the European AI Board supposed to be organised and run so that it remains neutral?
judge_reason: The answer quotes Art. 65(7) to state both the objectivity and impartiality requirements, and every structural claim (one representative per Member State, EDPS observer, AI Office without vote, Member State chair, AI Office secretariat, two-thirds rules of procedure) is supported by the given sources.
baseline_judge_reason: The answer states both key facts, quoting Art. 65(7) on safeguarding objectivity and impartiality, and its membership, voting, and chair details do not contradict the Act, though a stray German preamble sentence is a presentation flaw.
answer:
Article 65(7) states: “The Board shall be organised and operated so as to safeguard the objectivity and impartiality of its activities.” [AI Act Art. 65(7)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_65)

Its structure includes one representative per Member State; the European Data Protection Supervisor participates as an observer, and the AI Office attends without voting. [AI Act Art. 65(2)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_65) The Board is chaired by a Member State representative, while the AI Office provides the secretariat and prepares the agenda. [AI Act Art. 65(8)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_65)

Member State representatives adopt the rules of procedure by a two-thirds majority; those rules must cover matters including selection of the Chair and voting arrangements. [AI Act Art. 65(5)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_65)

*AI-generated answer (EU AI Act Art. 50(1)). Check the cited sources.*
baseline_answer:
Ich prüfe die einschlägigen Bestimmungen des AI Act direkt im amtlichen EU-Text, damit die Organisationsregeln und Neutralitätssicherungen präzise sind.

Under the AI Act, the Board’s neutrality is secured primarily through **nationally balanced membership, operating rules and an express duty of impartiality** [AI Act Art. 65(2)–(8)]:

- **One representative per Member State.** Each is designated for three years, renewable once. The European Data Protection Supervisor attends as an observer; the Commission’s AI Office attends but cannot vote. Other authorities, bodies or experts may be invited case by case.
- **Member-led rules.** The representatives adopt the Board’s rules of procedure by a two-thirds majority. Those rules cover the Chair’s selection and mandate, voting, and the organisation of the Board and its sub-groups.
- **A Member State representative chairs.** The AI Office provides the secretariat, convenes meetings at the Chair’s request and prepares the agenda under the Act and the rules of procedure.
- **Objectivity and impartiality are explicit requirements.** Article 65(7) says: “The Board shall be organised and operated so as to safeguard the objectivity and impartiality of its activities.”

The Act sets that requirement but does not prescribe a detailed conflict-of-interest process for Board members. Separately, it requires national competent authorities to exercise their powers independently, impartially and without bias [Art. 70(1)]. [Official AI Act text](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32024R1689)

question: When a company provides a general-purpose AI model to another company that builds it into its own AI system, what do they have to tell them about the training data?
judge_reason: The answer states all three key facts (training/testing/validation data, type and provenance, curation methodologies) with accurate wording from Annex XII 2(c), but the quoted text is attributed to Art. 53(1) when it actually comes from Annex XII, which Art. 53(1)(b)(ii) incorporates.

question: Can an AI system be put on the market in the EU without going through a conformity assessment, for example in an emergency?
judge_reason: The answer correctly covers the time-limited Art. 46(1) authorisation and the Art. 46(2) putting-into-service route, but it omits environmental protection and key infrastructure as grounds, and it never mentions that the Art. 46(2) authorisation must be requested during or after use without undue delay; its description of 46(2) also drops the public-security limb, though every cited claim is supported by the sources.
baseline_judge_reason: The answer declines to respond, but the key facts show the sources do cover the exception procedures, so a refusal states none of the expected facts.
answer:
Yes, but only under a limited derogation. Article 46(1) says that “any market surveillance authority may authorise the placing on the market or the putting into service” of a specific high-risk AI system on a duly justified request and for specified exceptional reasons, including public security or protecting people’s life and health. The authorisation is limited in time while the conformity assessment is completed, which must be done without undue delay. [AI Act Art. 46(1)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_46)

This is an exception to the usual requirement that the provider ensure the conformity assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service. [AI Act Art. 16(f)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_16) The market surveillance authority may authorise under Article 46(1) only if it concludes that the system complies with the requirements of Section 2. [AI Act Art. 46(3)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_46)

Article 46(2) provides a narrower emergency route for law-enforcement or civil-protection authorities to put a system into service without prior authorisation in a specific imminent threat to life or physical safety. That provision concerns putting into service, not placing on the market. [AI Act Art. 46(2)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_46)

question: Welche Behörden sind in Deutschland eigentlich dafür zuständig, Bußgeldverfahren wegen Verstößen gegen die KI-Verordnung durchzuführen?
judge_reason: The answer correctly names the market surveillance, notifying, and designated bodies for their own areas under § 17 Abs. 1 KI-MIG and adds the accurate § 2 Abs. 7 and § 17 Abs. 2 points, but its quote elides the case scope (§ 15 Abs. 1-2 and Art. 99 Abs. 3-5), so that key fact is only partly covered; every claim matches the given sources.
baseline_judge_reason: The answer covers the Marktüberwachungsbehörden, notifizierenden Behörden and Akkreditierungsstellen, the per-Geschäftsbereich responsibility, and the § 15 KI-MIG and Art. 99 Abs. 3–5 KI-VO scope, but omits the § 36 Abs. 1 Nr. 1 OWiG reference for the Verwaltungsbehörden.
answer:
Für die in § 17 Abs. 1 KI-MIG genannten Bußgeldfälle sind je nach Zuständigkeitsbereich **Marktüberwachungsbehörden, notifizierende Behörden und bestimmte Stellen** zuständig. Das Gesetz bestimmt: „Verwaltungsbehörden im Sinne des § 36 Absatz 1 Nummer 1 des Gesetzes über Ordnungswidrigkeiten sind […] die Marktüberwachungsbehörden nach § 2 Absatz 1 bis 8, die notifizierenden Behörden nach § 3 Absatz 1 und 2 Satz 1 und die Stellen nach § 3 Absatz 4 Satz 1 und 2 jeweils für ihren Geschäftsbereich.“ [KI-MIG § 17 Abs. 1](https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/ki-mig/__17.html)

Eine besondere Zuständigkeitsregel gilt für bestimmte Bundesfinanzbehörden und die Versorgungsanstalt des Bundes und der Länder: Die Bundesnetzagentur darf dort Durchsetzungsbefugnisse grundsätzlich nur im Einvernehmen mit dem Bundesministerium der Finanzen ausüben; kommt kein Einvernehmen zustande, geht die Marktüberwachungszuständigkeit für den Sachverhalt auf das Ministerium über. [KI-MIG § 2 Abs. 7](https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/ki-mig/__2.html)

Gegen Behörden und sonstige öffentliche Stellen im Sinne des Bundesdatenschutzgesetzes werden in den dort genannten Fällen keine Geldbußen verhängt. [KI-MIG § 17 Abs. 2](https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/ki-mig/__17.html)

baseline_answer:
Zuständig ist **nicht eine einzige zentrale Bußgeldbehörde**. Nach dem seit **29. Juli 2026** geltenden KI-MIG führen die Verwaltungsbehörden die Verfahren jeweils für ihren Geschäftsbereich: Das sind die zuständigen **Marktüberwachungsbehörden**, **notifizierenden Behörden** und bestimmte **Akkreditierungsstellen** (§ 17 Abs. 1 KI-MIG). Die Bußgeldvorschriften erfassen Verstöße nach § 15 KI-MIG sowie bestimmte Verstöße nach Art. 99 Abs. 3–5 der KI-Verordnung.

Im Regelfall ist die **Bundesnetzagentur** Marktüberwachungsbehörde. Je nach Fall sind jedoch andere Stellen zuständig, etwa **BaFin** für KI mit direktem Bezug zu regulierten Finanzaktivitäten, bestehende Fachbehörden für KI in regulierten Produktbereichen sowie Landesbehörden für bestimmte KI-Systeme öffentlicher Stellen oder Mediendienste (§ 2 KI-MIG). Bei Verstößen gegen Vorschriften zur Konformitätsbewertung können zudem die zuständigen notifizierenden Behörden oder Akkreditierungsstellen das Bußgeldverfahren führen.

Die Bundesnetzagentur ist außerdem zentrale Beschwerdestelle und leitet Beschwerden an die zuständige Stelle weiter; sie ist also nicht automatisch die Bußgeldbehörde in jedem Fall. **Gegen Behörden und sonstige öffentliche Stellen im Sinne des BDSG werden keine Geldbußen verhängt** (§ 17 Abs. 2 KI-MIG). [KI-MIG §§ 2, 8, 17](https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/ki-mig/BJNR0DF0B0026.html)

question: Welche Behörde überwacht in Deutschland die Einhaltung der KI-Regeln, wenn ein Medienunternehmen KI-Systeme für journalistische Inhalte oder für Werbung einsetzt, und gilt das auch für die Deutsche Welle?
judge_reason: The answer states both key facts, that market surveillance for media service providers lies with the state-law authorities and that the Deutsche Welle is supervised under the DW-Gesetz, and every claim and quote matches KI-MIG § 2 Abs. 8.
baseline_judge_reason: The answer states both key facts accurately (market surveillance by the Landesrecht-competent authorities, and the Deutsche Welle exception under the DW-Gesetz) with the correct legal reference and no contradictions, though its opening claim to have checked official sources is unverified.
answer:
Für Mediendienstanbieter, die KI-Systeme für journalistische oder Werbezwecke bei Mediendiensten einsetzen, liegt die Marktüberwachung bei den nach Landesrecht zuständigen Behörden. Das gilt, wenn sie die Systeme „bei der Veranstaltung, dem Angebot, der Verbreitung und der Zugänglichmachung von Mediendiensten“ in Verkehr bringen, in Betrieb nehmen oder verwenden. question: Mit wem sollen Anbieter von KI-Systemen mit allgemeinem Verwendungszweck nach Erwägungsgrund 85 der KI-Verordnung zusammenarbeiten, und warum?

question: Welche Kriterien berücksichtigt die Kommission nach Anhang XIII der KI-Verordnung bei der Benennung von KI-Modellen mit allgemeinem Verwendungszweck mit systemischem Risiko?

baseline_judge_reason: The answer states all seven expected key facts (parameters, dataset size in tokens, training compute, modalities, benchmarks, market reach with the 10,000 business-user threshold, and registered end-users) with no contradictions, and its extra details match Annex XIII.
answer:
Die bereitgestellten Auszüge nennen folgende Kriterien:

- „die Anzahl der Parameter des Modells“ [Annex XIII a](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/DE/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#anx_XIII)

question: Welche Rolle sollen Praxisleitfäden nach Erwägungsgrund 135 der KI-Verordnung bei der Kennzeichnung KI-erzeugter Inhalte spielen?
judge_reason: The answer covers the purpose, practical measures, and the public-recognition goal, and correctly states that the codes do not affect the binding nature of the transparency duties, but it omits that the Commission facilitates and promotes drafting the codes.
baseline_judge_reason: The answer covers the Commission's role in facilitating codes of practice, the detection and cooperation measures, the public-recognition goal, and the unchanged binding transparency duties, but it omits the key fact about disseminating content and verifying authenticity and origin.
answer:
Praxisleitfäden sollen die wirksame Umsetzung der Pflichten zur Feststellung und Kennzeichnung KI-erzeugter oder manipulierter Inhalte unterstützen. Sie können praktische Vorkehrungen fördern, etwa zugängliche Feststellungsmechanismen, Zusammenarbeit entlang der Wertschöpfungskette sowie die Verbreitung und Echtheits- oder Herkunftsprüfung von Inhalten, damit die Öffentlichkeit KI-erzeugte Inhalte wirksam erkennen kann. Die Leitfäden ändern dabei nichts am verbindlichen Charakter und der uneingeschränkten Anwendbarkeit der Transparenzpflichten. [Recital 135](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/DE/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32024R1689#rct_135)

Praxisleitfäden sollen die **praktische Umsetzung** der Pflichten zur Erkennung und Kennzeichnung KI-generierter oder manipulierter Inhalte erleichtern. Sie können etwa dazu beitragen, Erkennungsmechanismen zugänglich zu machen und die Zusammenarbeit entlang der Wertschöpfungskette zu fördern, damit die Öffentlichkeit KI-Inhalte besser von anderen unterscheiden kann.

Erwägungsgrund 135 betont zugleich, dass solche Leitfäden die **verbindlichen Transparenzpflichten weder ersetzen noch abschwächen**. Die Kommission kann ihre Erstellung auf Unionsebene fördern und unterstützen. [Erwägungsgrund 135 der KI-Verordnung](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32024R1689)

question: Unter welchen Voraussetzungen gilt nach Art. 42 Abs. 2 KI-VO die Vermutung, dass ein Hochrisiko-KI-System die Cybersicherheitsanforderungen erfüllt?
judge_reason: The answer covers all three key facts and quotes Art. 42(2) accurately, but it wrongly says the system's own Fundstelle must be published in the Official Journal, when the source requires publication of the certification scheme's references.
baseline_judge_reason: The answer covers all three key facts: certification under an EU 2019/881 scheme with an OJ-published reference or a conformity declaration, the presumption of meeting Art. 15 cybersecurity requirements, and the limit to requirements covered by the certificate or declaration, in whole or part.
answer:
Die Vermutung gilt, wenn das Hochrisiko-KI-System im Rahmen eines Cybersicherheitszertifizierungssystems nach der Verordnung (EU) 2019/881 zertifiziert wurde oder eine entsprechende Konformitätserklärung erstellt wurde, die Fundstelle des Systems im Amtsblatt der EU veröffentlicht wurde und die Zertifizierung oder Erklärung die betreffenden Anforderungen ganz oder teilweise abdeckt:

> „Für Hochrisiko-KI-Systeme, die im Rahmen eines der Cybersicherheitszertifizierungssysteme gemäß der Verordnung (EU) 2019/881, deren Fundstellen im Amtsblatt der Europäischen Union veröffentlicht wurden, zertifiziert wurden oder für die eine solche Konformitätserklärung erstellt wurde, gilt die Vermutung, dass sie die in Artikel 15 der vorliegenden Verordnung festgelegten Cybersicherheitsanforderungen erfüllen, sofern diese Anforderungen von der Cybersicherheitszertifizierung oder der Konformitätserklärung oder Teilen davon abdeckt sind.“ [AI Act Art. 42(2)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/DE/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_42)

question: Wofür muss ein Akteur nach Art. 79 Abs. 4 KI-VO sorgen, wenn sein KI-System ein Risiko birgt, und für welche KI-Systeme gilt das?
judge_reason: The answer states all three expected facts (take all appropriate corrective measures, covering all affected AI systems the actor placed on the EU market) with the Art. 79(4) wording, and its scope claim about risky products matches Art. 79(1) in the sources.

answer:
Der Akteur muss „alle geeigneten Korrekturmaßnahmen in Bezug auf alle betreffenden KI-Systeme, die er auf dem Unionsmarkt bereitgestellt hat“, treffen lassen. [AI Act Art. 79(4)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/DE/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_79)

Das gilt für KI-Systeme, die als Produkte mit einem Risiko gelten, sofern sie Risiken für die Gesundheit oder Sicherheit oder die Grundrechte von Personen bergen. [AI Act Art. 79(1)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/DE/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_79)

question: Welche Verfahrensvorschriften gelten nach § 16 Abs. 2 KI-MIG für Verfahren wegen Verstößen nach Art. 99 Abs. 3 bis 5 KI-VO, und was gilt für eine Einstellung durch die Staatsanwaltschaft?

question: Wie wird eine geeignete Konformitätsbewertungsstelle nach dem KI-MIG notifiziert, und was verlangt der Artikel der KI-Verordnung, auf den es dabei verweist?
judge_reason: The answer covers the KI-MIG § 3 Abs. 3 grant of authority, the notification to the Commission and member states, and the suspensive condition, but omits the Art. 30(2) details (Anhang XIV and the Commission's electronic notification tool) and instead focuses on Art. 30(1) and (3); every claim is supported by the given sources.
baseline_judge_reason: The answer correctly states the conditional authorization and the notification to the Commission and member states via the electronic tool, but it omits Anhang XIV and misidentifies the referenced article as Art. 28 Abs. 1 instead of Art. 30 Abs. 2.
answer:
Nach § 3 Abs. 3 KI-MIG prüft die zuständige notifizierende Behörde, ob die Konformitätsbewertungsstelle die Anforderungen des Artikels 31 erfüllt. Bei positivem Ergebnis erteilt sie ihr die Befugnis zu Konformitätsbewertungen und notifiziert sie der Kommission und den übrigen Mitgliedstaaten. Die Befugnis ist unter der aufschiebenden Bedingung zu erteilen, dass weder die Kommission noch andere Mitgliedstaaten Einwände erheben. [KI-MIG § 3 Abs. 3](https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/ki-mig/__3.html)

Für Hochrisiko-KI-Systeme nach Artikel 6 Absatz 2 in Verbindung mit Anhang III Nummer 1 ist die nach Artikel 52 Absatz 2 der Verordnung (EU) 2024/2847 zu benennende Marktüberwachungsbehörde zuständig; bis zu ihrer Benennung nimmt diese Aufgabe das BSI wahr. [KI-MIG § 3 Abs. 2](https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/ki-mig/__3.html)

Artikel 30 verlangt, dass nur Stellen notifiziert werden, die Artikel 31 erfüllen: „Die notifizierenden Behörden dürfen nur Konformitätsbewertungsstellen notifizieren, die die Anforderungen des Artikels 31 erfüllen.“ [AI Act Art. 30(1)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/DE/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_30) Die Notifizierung muss Angaben zu Tätigkeiten, Modulen, Arten von KI-Systemen und Kompetenzbestätigung enthalten. Beruht sie nicht auf einer Akkreditierungsurkunde, sind zusätzlich Nachweise der Kompetenz und der regelmäßigen Überwachung vorzulegen. [AI Act Art. 30(3)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/DE/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_30)

Die konkreten Anforderungen des Artikels 31 sind in den vorliegenden Quellen nicht wiedergegeben.

Dann erteilt sie der Stelle die Befugnis, Konformitätsbewertungen vorzunehmen, und notifiziert sie der EU-Kommission und den übrigen Mitgliedstaaten über das elektronische Notifizierungsinstrument. Die Befugnis kann mit Auflagen oder befristet erteilt werden; sie steht unter dem Vorbehalt, dass Kommission und Mitgliedstaaten keine Einwände erheben. Diese ist für die Verfahren zur Bewertung, Benennung und Notifizierung der Stellen sowie für deren Überwachung zuständig. Die Verfahren werden mit den notifizierenden Behörden der anderen Mitgliedstaaten abgestimmt. [Art. 28 KI-Verordnung](https://www.buzer.de/28_KI-VO.htm)

Für den Antrag der Stelle und die Angaben zur Notifizierung regeln Art. 29 und 30 KI-Verordnung die Einzelheiten; die Eignungsanforderungen an die Stelle selbst stehen in Art. 31.

ISO/IEC 42001:2023 requires an organization to establish, implement, maintain, and continually improve an AI management system (AIMS). It applies to organizations of any size that provide or use AI products or services. [ISO/IEC 42001:2023](https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/90574)

In practice, the AIMS must cover:

- **Organizational context and leadership:** identify relevant internal and external issues and interested parties; set an AI policy, assign responsibilities, and provide resources.
- **Planning:** identify and assess AI risks and impacts, decide how to address them, and set AI objectives.
- **Support and operation:** provide needed competence, awareness, and documented information; control relevant AI processes and the AI system life cycle, including external suppliers.
- **Evaluation and improvement:** monitor and evaluate performance, conduct internal audits and management reviews, and correct problems while continually improving the system.

Annex A provides reference controls in areas such as AI policy, roles, resources, impact assessment, life-cycle management, data, transparency, use, and third-party relationships. Organizations select controls based on their risks and document their choices in a statement of applicability; the standard allows controls to be excluded with justification or supplemented as needed. [ISO/IEC 42001:2023](https://cdn.standards.iteh.ai/samples/81230/4c1911ebc9a641fcb6ee21aa09c28ad3/ISO-IEC-42001-2023.pdf)

answer:
Some older GSM ciphers, such as A5/1 and A5/2, are known to be vulnerable; commercial tools can decrypt calls in real time. [CAPEC-608](https://capec.mitre.org/data/definitions/608.html) Newer UMTS and LTE encryption is stronger and believed less vulnerable to these attacks. [CAPEC-608](https://capec.mitre.org/data/definitions/608.html)

However, an attacker using a rogue base station—or cooperating with a malicious mobile network operator—can force a phone to use no encryption or easily breakable encryption. [CAPEC-606](https://capec.mitre.org/data/definitions/606.html) A rogue base station can also force newer phones to use weak cellular encryption. [CAPEC-608](https://capec.mitre.org/data/definitions/608.html)

---

baseline_answer:
Yes, **legacy 2G GSM encryption is substantially weaker** than the algorithms used by UMTS (3G) and LTE (4G). GSM’s commonly deployed A5/1 cipher has practical weaknesses, and A5/2 is considered broken. UMTS and LTE use newer, generally stronger algorithms; public guidance has not identified comparable weaknesses in their core air-interface ciphers. That does not mean every call is encrypted end to end: cellular encryption protects the radio link, and security also depends on network configuration and what happens beyond the base station. [NIST’s LTE security guide](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/specialpublications/nist.sp.800-187.pdf)

**A downgrade can be possible.** A rogue base station may trick a phone into connecting through an older network generation, where weaker GSM protection could be negotiated. This depends on the phone, network, coverage and configuration; it is not guaranteed that an attacker can force every phone to use GSM. [NIST Mobile Threat Catalogue: CEL-3](https://pages.nist.gov/mobile-threat-catalogue/cellular-threats/CEL-3.html) [CAPEC-606](https://capec.mitre.org/data/definitions/606.html)

In practice, use end-to-end encrypted calling for sensitive conversations. That protects call content even if the cellular radio link is downgraded.

question: How would an attacker use a malicious web server to exploit a buffer overflow in a client program like a browser, and what decides whether this only crashes the software or lets the attacker run code?

Whether the result is only a crash or code execution depends on how the overflow content is crafted: excessive or random data may crash the program, while a targeted payload that overwrites the return address with a value chosen by the attacker can redirect execution and potentially run arbitrary code. [CAPEC-14](https://capec.mitre.org/data/definitions/14.html) The targeted code-execution case requires greater skill than merely causing a crash. *AI-generated answer (EU AI Act Art. 50(1)). Check the cited sources.*
baseline_answer:

question: What happens when software gives a user or component more privileges than it should have, and how can developers limit the damage?

answer:

It can also expose new weaknesses or magnify the impact of existing ones. [CWE-266](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/266.html) [CWE-250](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/250.html)

Developers can limit the damage by:

- Following **least privilege**: grant only the permissions needed, and use isolated, task-specific accounts where possible. [CWE-269](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/269.html) [CWE-250](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/250.html)
- Defining trust zones and separating privileged code from other functionality; require multiple conditions before granting access to sensitive resources. [CWE-266](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/266.html) [CWE-270](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/270.html)
- Raising privileges only when necessary, dropping them promptly, and checking that privilege changes succeeded. [CWE-250](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/250.html)
- Validating input to any privileged code and handling failed access checks or operations safely. [CWE-250](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/250.html) [CWE-280](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/280.html)

answer:
People hide prompts in content the agent reads, such as emails and documents, using:

- **Visually hidden text:** tiny font, text matching the background, or hidden HTML elements. [AML.T0068](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0068)

- **Obfuscation:** encoding instructions with schemes such as Base64 or ROT13. [AML.T0068](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0068)

The agent may process those instructions even when a person doesn’t notice them; a crafted email, for example, can silently trigger hidden instructions. [T1698](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1698) [ASI01](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/)

baseline_answer:
People usually hide them in **content the AI reads but a person may overlook**: white or tiny text, text behind images, HTML comments or hidden elements, document metadata, and email quoting or attachments. The hidden text might tell an agent to ignore its instructions, reveal data, or take an action. This is a form of indirect prompt injection; MITRE ATLAS tracks it as [AML.T0051](https://atlas.mitre.org/techniques/AML.T0051/).

For defense, treat documents and emails as **untrusted input**: don’t let their instructions override the agent’s rules, restrict what tools and data the agent can access, and require confirmation before consequential actions.
